newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown weakens ignoring govt showing in vote.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown weakens ignoring govt showing in vote.

text.p: The Czech crown weakened slightly on Monday and was seen losing more ground throughout the week, apparently ignoring a strong showing by the centre-right governing coalition in Senate elections at the weekend.
Analysts said the slide was fuelled by short-term position closing by London-based operators after last week's gains in the run-off to the election.
In late afternoon trading, the crown was trading at 26.849 against the dollar and 17.679 against the mark, implying a deviation of +3.10 percent against the basket mid-point after +3.30 percent open.

"The (decline) surprised us a bit. The crown has proven this morning not to be so strong (as on Friday), and has returned to the level at which it really should be, perhaps it could gently extend its losses throughout the week," Jakub Perina, a dealer at bank CSOB, told Reuters.
Jaromir Cerny of Zivnostenska Banka said:
"The crown will probably lose some of last week's gains, weakening by up to 50 basis points throughout the week, which is due to a short-term position closing."
"In my view, the crown today did not react to the elections at all," he added.
The central bank followed the market trend on Monday, fixing the crown at 26.785 to the dollar after Friday's fixing at 26.553, and at 17.694 to the mark from 17.717.
The above rates imply a deviation from the midpoint of the central bank's mark/dollar basket of +3.13 percent, after a deviation of +3.33 on Friday.

The minority coalition of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus took 52 of 81 seats in the newly-created upper house of parliament, following the second round of voting, well ahead of the centre-left opposition Social Democrats which took 25 seats.

The Senate is a mostly advisory body with limited legislative powers, but the election was the first test at the polls for Klaus since his coalition lost its lower house majority in general elections in June.
